chunks.content: 96 The #1 Closing Mistake That Could Wreck Your Deal (And How to Avoid It) Hi Sara, Let’s talk about a sneaky little deal-killer: closing mechanics. I know, I know—sounds like something only lawyers and escrow agents should care about. But if you’re buying or selling an accounting firm (or any business, really), this is the one thing you cannot afford to mess up. See, your agreements are written based on a plan for closing. If everyone (buyer, seller, and lawyers) isn’t on the same page about what that looks like, things can go sideways—fast. Two Ways to Close a Deal (And Why It Matters) Most people assume that when you sign a purchase agreement, boom! The deal is done. That’s the old-school, “simultaneous sign and close” approach. No difference between the signing date, closing date, and effective date—it’s all one and the same. Simple, right? Except when it’s not. Banks and state agencies love to complicate things. Okay okay, so do lawyers! But get a load of this chicken and egg situation: Most lenders won’t schedule your closing until they see a final approved (and sometimes) signed purchase agreement. Sometimes the lender won’t close until you get a state agency’s sign off, but in order to get that sign off, the state requires a signed agreement. So somehow you need to sign the purchase agreement BEFORE you can actually confirm you have the money to purchase the business. So if you’re relying on financing, you’d better believe you need an escape hatch in case the bank pulls the plug at the last second (which certainly happened in 2020). That’s why we almost always structure deals as a delayed sign-and-close. The idea? You sign the purchase agreement as soon as both parties are ready. You close at a later date, once financing, tax clearances, and other conditions are met. There are built-in escape clauses (a.k.a. “conditions precedent”) so nobody gets stuck in a deal they can’t afford to close. What Actually Happens on Closing Day? So if you’ve already signed the purchase agreement, what’s left to do at closing? Glad you asked. On closing day, you’ll finalize: ✔ The Wire Transfer – Because sellers don’t work on the honor system. ✔ The Promissory Note – A legally binding “I.O.U.” that shouldn’t be signed until we are really sure things are going the distance. ✔ The Bill of Sale – Officially transfers ownership. ✔ Assignment & Assumption Agreements – Ensures the buyer is stepping into the seller’s legal shoes. ✔ The Closing Certificate – A final “truth check” that confirms everything the seller promised originally is still true on closing day. Mess this up, and you could be in for a world of legal and financial headaches. The Bottom Line If you’re buying or selling an accounting practice, get clear on your closing mechanics early. A sloppy approach can lead to unnecessary risk, frustrated buyers and sellers, and even lawsuits. To smooth deals and stress-free closings, Sara Sharp Partner, SK&S Law Group Business Consultant and Founder of Deal Academy P.S.
